title: Exenatide prevents fat-induced insulin resistance and raises adiponectin expression and plasma levels.
text_summary: 本研究在高脂饮食大鼠中考察长期艾塞那肽治疗对葡萄糖耐量、胰岛素敏感性、胰岛素信号和脂肪细胞因子的影响。艾塞那肽抑制了高脂饮食引起的体重、游离脂肪酸、甘油三酯和总胆固醇升高，并改善静脉葡萄糖耐量、外周及肝脏胰岛素敏感性、胰岛素清除和脂肪及骨骼肌IRS-1酪氨酸磷酸化。治疗还降低循环内脂素，同时提高脂联素基因表达和血浆水平。结果表明，慢性艾塞那肽可防止高脂饮食诱导的胰岛素抵抗，其作用与体重和脂质改善、胰岛素信号恢复及脂肪细胞因子改变有关。

ORIGINAL ARTICLE doi: 10.1111/j.1463-1326.2007.00832.x
Exenatide prevents fat-induced insulin resistance and raises
adiponectin expression and plasma levels
L. Li, 1* G. Yang, 2* Q. Li, 2 X. Tan, 1 H. Liu, 3 Y. Tang 4 and G. Boden 5
1Department of Clinical Biochemistry in Chongqing Medical University and The Key Laboratory of Laboratory Medical Diag-
nostics in the Ministry of Education, Chongqing, China
2Department of Endocrinology, The Second Affiliated Hospital, Chongqing Medical University, Chongqing, China
3Department of Pediatrics, University of Mississippi Medical Center, Jackson, MS, USA
4Oncology Research, Centocor, Inc., Malvern, PA, USA
5The Division of Endocrinology/Diabetes/Metabolism and the Clinical Research Center, Temple University School of Medicine,
Philadelphia, PA, USA
Background: Exenatide (exendin-4) can reduce blood glucose levels, increase insulin secretion and improve insulin
sensitivity through mechanisms that are not completely understood.
Methods: In the present study, we examined the effects of exenatide treatment on glucose tolerance (intravenous
glucose tolerance test), insulin sensitivity (euglycaemic–hyperinsulinaemic clamps), insulin signalling (insulin
receptor substrate 1 tyrosine phosphor ylation) and adipocytokine levels (visfatin and adiponectin) in high fat–fed
rats.
Results: Administration of exenatide (0.5 or 2.0 mg/kg twice daily /C2 6 weeks) prevented high-fat diet (HFD)–induced
increases in body weight, plasma free fatty acids, triglycerides and total cholesterol. Exenatide also prevented HFD-
induced deterioration in peripheral and hepatic insulin sensitivity, insulin clearance, glucose tolerance and decreased
tyrosine phosphorylation of insulin receptor substrate-1 (IRS-1) in fat and skeletal muscles. Interestingly, plasma
visfatin levels decreased in exenatide-treated rats, whereas expression and plasma levels of adiponectin increased.
Conclusions: These results indicate that chronic exenatide treatment enhances insulin sensitivity and protects against
high fat–induced insulin resistance.
Keywords: adiponectin, exenatide, insulin sensitivity, visfatin
Received 19 October 2007; accepted 2 November 2007
Introduction
Glucagon-like peptide (GLP)-1 is secreted from the
intestinal mucosa in response to meal ingestion. Phys-
iological GLP-1 levels increase glucose-stimulated
insulin secretion, suppress glucagon secretion, delay
gastric emptying, reduce food intake and may promote
b-cell preservation and neogenesis [1,2]. These actions
have fostered considerable interest in the use of GLP-1
for the treatment of type 2 diabetes. Unfortunately,
GLP-1 has an extremely short plasma half-life of 1–
2m i n .
Exendin-4, a peptide produced in the salivary glands of
the Gila monster ( Heloderma suspectum ), is a 39 amino
acid peptide that has been shown to be a potent agonist
of the GLP-1 receptor [3–5]. Exendin-4 has a longer
plasma half-life and is a more potent insulinotropic
agent than GLP-1 [6–10].

Exenatide and GLP-1 share many glucoregulatory activ-
ities, including glucose-dependent enhancement of insu-
lin secretion [7,11–13], suppression of glucagon
secretion [12,14,15], slowing of gastric emptying [14]
and reduction of food intake [16]. In addition, exenatide
has been shown to restore first-phase insulin secretion
[17,18] and promote b-cell proliferation and islet neo-
genesis in animal models [3].
The mechanism by which exenatide increases insulin
sensitivity in animal models of diabetes [3,14,19]
including the Zucker diabetic fatty rat has remained
uncertain. It was the objective of the present study to
investigate effects of exenatide, administered twice
daily for 6 weeks to rats with high fat–induced insulin
resistance, on glucose and lipid metabolism, insulin sig-
nalling and adipocytokine expression.
Research Design and Methods
Animals
Seventy male Sprague–Dawley rats aged 4 weeks and
weighing between 120 and 130 g were purchased from
the Experimental Animal Center of Chongqing Medical
University (Chongqing, China). The rats were housed in
individual cages in a temperature-controlled room with
a 12-h light/dark cycle, where they had free access to
standard rat chow and water. After 3 days, the rats were
randomly divided into two groups (figure 1). One group
was fed a normal chow diet (NC, n ¼ 20) containing
60% carbohydrate, 21% protein, 19% fat, fibres, vita-
mins and minerals. The other group was fed a high-fat
diet (n ¼ 50) containing 54% fat, 33% carbohydrate
and 13% protein with quantities of fibres, vitamins
and minerals equal to those in the standard diet. After
10 weeks, rats fed the high-fat diet were subdivided
into three groups (figure 1). One group was given exe-
natide (Amylin Corporation, San Diego, CA, USA) at
a dose of 0.5 mg/kg twice daily (HFL). The second
group received exenatide at a dose of 2 mg/kg twice
daily (HE), and the third group was given saline (HF).
All injections were given intraperitoneally twice daily
in a volume of 0.5 ml for 6 weeks (figure 1). All exper-
imental procedures were approved by the Animal
Experimentation Ethics Committee (Chongqing Medi-
cal University) and were in accordance with the
National Health and Medical Research Council of
China Guidelines on Animal Experimentation.
Surgical Procedure
Five to seven days before the studies, rats were anaes-
thetized with an intraperitoneal injection of pentobarbi-
tal (50 mg/kg, Nembutal; Abbott Laboratories, Abbott
Park, IL, USA). A silastic catheter (ID ¼ 0.02 inch) was
inserted into the right internal jugular vein and
extended to the level of the right atrium. Another cath-
eter was advanced through the left carotid artery until
its tip reached the aortic arch. The free ends of both
catheters were attached to long segments of steel tubing
and tunnelled subcutaneously around the side of the
neck to the back of the neck where they were exterior-
ized through a skin incision and then securely anchored
to the skin by a standard wounded clip. At the end of
the procedure, catheters were flushed with 300 mlo f
isotonic saline containing heparin (20 U/ml) and ampi-
cillin (5 mg/ml) and then filled with a viscous solution
of heparin (300 U/ml) and 80% polyvinylpyrollidone
(PVP-10; Fisher Scientific, Pittsburgh, PA, USA) to pre-
vent refluxing of blood into the catheter lumen.
Intravenous Glucose Tolerance and Insulin
Tolerance Test
Overnight-fasted rats were given i.v. glucose (0.5 g/kg
body weight), and vein blood was collected before (time
0 min) and at indicated times after injection for mea-
surement of glucose (Bayer, Amsterdam, Netherland,
Glucometer Elite) and insulin. For the insulin tolerance
test (ITT), 6-h-fasted rats were injected with 0.75 U
human insulin/kg body weight (Novolin R; Novo Nor-
disk, Copenhagen, Denmark). Blood samples were col-
lected after 0, 5, 10, 20 and 30 min for measurement of
glucose.

Euglycaemic–hyperinsulinaemic Clamps
Euglycaemic–hyperinsulinaemic clamps were per-
formed with awake and unrestrained rats as described
[21]. Briefly, glucose concentrations were clamped at
euglycaemic levels by a variable rate infusion of 25%
glucose. Blood glucose levels were monitored with
a portable glucometer, and glucose infusion rates (GIRs)
were adjusted every 5–10 min as needed. [3-
3H]glucose
(Amersham, Los Angeles, CA, USA) was infused
through the jugular vein catheter starting at 0 min
with a bolus (6 mCi) followed by a continuous infusion
(0.2 mCi/min /C2 3 h). Insulin (4.8 mU/kg/min) was in-
fused through the carotid artery catheter from 60 to
180 min during euglycaemic–hyperinsulinaemic clamps.
Blood samples (400 ml) were obtained from the jugular
vein at 0, 60, 140, 160, 170 and 180 min for determina-
tion of insulin, adiponectin, visfatin, free fatty acids
(FFA) and specific activity of titrated glucose. Each
blood sample was replaced by the same volume of fresh
whole blood from a donor rat. After the last blood sam-
pling at 180 min, animals were killed with a lethal dose
of sodium pentobarbital (80 mg/kg), and samples of
muscle and epididymal white adipose tissue (WAT)
were excised, immediately quick-frozen and stored at
/C0 80 °C for subsequent analyses.
Analytical Procedures
Plasma insulin was measured in deproteinized serum by
radioimmunoassay using rat insulin as standard (Linco,
St Charles, MO, USA). FFA was measured in plasma
with a kit from Wako Pure Chemicals (Richmond, VA,
USA). Plasma glucose specific activity was measured in
duplicate after zinc sulphate and barium hydroxide
deproteinization. Adiponectin was measured by plasma
containing EDTA (1 mg/ml of blood) and a protease inhib-
itor (Aprotinin, 100 U/ml of blood) by enzyme-linked
immunosorbent assay (Phoenix Pharmaceuticals, Bel-
mont, CA, USA). The limit of detection was 0.25 ng/ml,
intra-assay co-efficients of variation were 6.4% and inter-
assay co-efficients of variation were 7.0%. Plasma visfatin
protein was measured by Western blotting (Santa Cruz
Biotechnology, Santa Cruz, CA, USA).
RT-PCR Analysis of Gene Expression
Total RNA was isolated from WAT or muscle using Trizol
reagent (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA, USA). Reverse tran-
scription was performed on 1 mg total RNA using RTase
M-MLV (RNAse H
/C0 , TaKaRa Bio, Dalian, China) and
Oligo (dT)18 Primer (TaKaRa Bio, Dalian, China). PCR
assays were performed using Taq DNA polymerase,
including 10 pmol of each primer in a master mix of
50 ml of the following primers: visfatin (5 ¢ primer, 5 ¢-
TTCTTGTCCAGTCCT GGTATCCA-3 ¢;3 ¢ primer, 5 ¢-
TCCCGCCACAGTAT CT GTTCCTT-3 ¢), adiponectin
(5¢ primer, 5¢-ATGTTCCCATTCGCTTTACT-3¢;3 ¢ primer,
5¢-TCGCCTGTTCTTTGATTCTC-3¢), PPAR g (5¢ primer,
5¢-GATGACCAC TCCCATTCCTTTG-3 ¢;3 ¢ primer, 5 ¢-
GATGCTTTATC CCCACAGACTC-3 ¢), insulin receptor
(InsR: 5 ¢ primer, 5 ¢-CTTCAAACCCAGAG TACCTCA-3 ¢;
3¢ primer, 5 ¢-GTCATTCCAAAGTCTCCGATT-3¢), IRS-1
(5¢ primer, 5 ¢-CCTGACATTGGA GGTGGGTCTT-3 ¢;3 ¢
primer, 5 ¢-GAATCTTCGGCAGTTGC GGTAT-3 ¢), phos-
phatidyline itol 3 Kinase (PI3K) (5 ¢ primer, 5¢-GCAGAT-
GCTTTCAAACGCTAT-3¢;3 ¢ primer, 5 ¢-CACTCCACTC
CGCTGAGATTA-3¢), glucose transporter-4 (GLUT-4)
(5¢ primer, 5 ¢-AGCCAGCCTACG C CACCATA-3 ¢;
3¢ primer, 5 ¢-GGACCCATAGCATCCGCAA C-3 ¢) and
housekeeper b-actin (5 ¢ primer, 5 ¢-GACCCAGATCATG-
TTTGAGACC-3¢;3¢ primer, 5¢-GCAGTAATCTCCTTCTG-
CATCC-3¢).
Reactions were performed in a 40- ml volume including
diluted complementary DNA sample (6 ml) and primers
(4 ml). Samples were incubated for an initial denatura-
tion at 94 °C for 3 min for one PCR cycle. In the fol-
lowing cycles, each cycle consisted of 94 °C for 30 s
for degeneration, 55 °C for 30 s for annealing, 72 °C
for 40 s for extension and different cycles for each
gene. Eventually, one PCR cycling was performed at
72 °C for 5 min for intense extension. The intensities
of PCR bands were quantified with a Bio Imaging Sys-
tem Densitometer (Bio-Rad, CA, USA).
IRS-1 Tyrosine Phosphorylation Assays
To investigate the effects of exenatide on insulin-
stimulated tyrosine phosphorylation, rats were studied
after 6 weeks of exenatide treatment and compared
with pair-fed controls. To maximally stimulate protein
tyrosine phosphorylation in adipose and muscle tissues,
insulin was injected through cardiac puncture at the
dose of 0.5 U/kg body weight, and epididymal WAT
and muscles were rapidly harvested after 5 min and
frozen in liquid N
2.
For dot-blot assays, 100 mg of muscle or adipose tissue
was homogenized in liquid nitrogen and treated with
lysis buffer (150 mmol/l NaCl, 1% NP-40, 0.5% deoxy-
cholic acid sodium and 50 mmol/l Tris, pH 8.0). The
lysates were clarified by centrifugation (20 000 g at 4 °C
for 3 min). Hundred microlitres of supernatant was blot-
ted onto the PVDF membrane (0.22 mm) by vacuum using
a Bio-Dot blotting apparatus (Bio-Rad). The membrane

was blocked with buffer A (TBST 50 mM Tris, pH 7.5,

120 min. The membrane was incubated for 2 h at 30 °C
in buffer A containing a rabbit anti-IRS-1 phosphotyr-

technology). The membrane was then washed three
times with TBST for 10 min before being incubated for
30 min at 30 °C with horseradish peroxidase–labelled
sheep antirabbit immunoglobulin G (IgG) antibody
(Santa Cruz Biotechnology, CA, USA) diluted 1 : 5000
in TBST. Washing in TBST was repeated as described
above, and the reactive dots were identified after a 5-
min incubation in enhanced chemiluminescence (ECL),
prepared according to the manufacturer’s instructions.
The intensity of the dots was quantified with a Bio
Imaging System Densitometer (Bio-Rad, CA, USA).
Calculations
Glucose rates of appearance (G
Ra) were determined with
3-[3H] glucose as described [21]. G Ra and the glucose
rate of disappearance (G Rd) were calculated using the
non-steady–state equation of Steele et al. [22]. The dis-
tribution volume for glucose was assumed to be 150 mg/
kg. Hepatic glucose production (HGP) was calculated as
the difference between the isotopically determined G
Ra
and the rate of glucose infused to maintain euglycaemia
(GIR). HGP ¼ G
Ra /C0 GIR. K values of glucose disappear-
ance were calculated as 70/t 1/2 during the 5–60-min
period of the intravenous glucose tolerance test (IVGTT)
glucose responses [23].
Statistical Analysis
Data are presented as means /C6 s.e. A repeated measures
analysis of variance was used to assess the results mea-
sured at consecutive multiple time points. A two-way
design was used to incorporate additional effects of
different experimental groups followed by a post hoc
protected least significant difference (PLSD) test to
compare two individual groups. Within-group compar-
isons were made using the paired Student’s t-test. Dif-
ferences were statistically significant at p < 0.05. All
analyses were performed using
SPSS (SPSS graduate
pack; SPSS, Chicago, IL, USA).
Results
Basal Metabolic Parameters
The high-fat diet (HFD) significantly increased body
weight (from 359 to 453 g, p < 0.01) as well as plasma
concentrations of FFA, triglycerides and total cholesterol.
Plasma glucose concentrations did not change, whereas
plasma insulin levels tended to increase. The low-
dose exenatide (0.5 mg/kg) partially reduced the HFD-
mediated weight gain and the increases in triglyceride
and total cholesterol, whereas the high-dose exenatide
(2.0 mg/kg) resulted in complete normalization of the
HFD-induced changes in body weight, plasma FFA, tri-
glyceride and total cholesterol (table 1).
Effect of HFD and Exenatide on IVGTT
The peak glucose levels achieved over the first 15 min of
the IVGTT were significantly higher in HF and HFL than
in NC and HE rats (figure 2). Plasma glucose levels retu-
rned back to baseline within 30 min in both exenatide-
treated and control rats, while the return to baseline
was delayed in HF rats. The K values of glucose disap-
pearance during the IVGTT were significantly lower in
the HF than in the NC and HE groups (3.36 /C6 0.12 vs.
3.77 /C6 0.11 and 4.07 /C6 0.22, both p < 0.05). Insulin

basal values. Despite identical insulin infusion rates
(4.8 mU/kg min), plasma insulin levels were higher in the
HF rats than in the exenatide-treated and control rats
(p < 0.01). Hyperinsulinaemia suppressed plasma FFA

Effects of Exenatide on InsR, PI3K, IRS-1 and
GLUT4 mRNA Expression
The messenger RNA (mRNA) expression of InsR, IRS-1,
PI3K and GLUT4 in adipose and muscle tissue was not
different among the three groups (data not shown).
Effects of Exenatide on IRS-1 Tyrosine
Phosphorylation
The tyrosine phosphorylation level of IRS-1 in adipose
and muscle tissue from HF rats was decreased compared
with controls (adipose: 0.50 /C6 0.03 vs. 0.59 /C6 0.03%;
muscle: 0.73 /C6 0.03 vs. 0.82 /C6 0.05%). This defect was
corrected in exenatide-treated rat tissue (0.57 /C6 0.02 and
0.81 /C6 0.03%, figure 5a, b).
Effects of Exenatide on Adiponectin mRNA and
Plasma Levels
Adiponectin mRNA content in WAT was lower in the HF
rats than in the controls (0.51 /C6 0.04 vs. 0.77 /C6 0.04 arbi-
trary units, p < 0.01) and higher than in NC in exenatide-
treated rats (1.01 /C6 0.06 vs. 0.77 /C6 0.05 arbitrary units,
both p < 0.01, figure 5d).
Compared with the control rats, plasma adiponectin
levels in HF rats tended to be lower (0.50 /C6 0.02 vs.
0.55 /C6 0.01 mg/l). In high-dose exenatide–treated rats,
plasma adiponectin was significantly higher than in the
controls (0.75 /C6 0.02 vs. 0.55 /C6 0.01 mg/l, p < 0.01,
table 1).
Effects of Exenatide Treatment on the Expression
of Visfatin mRNA and its Plasma Protein Levels
Plasma visfatin protein level was highest in controls
(1.17 /C6 0.24 optical density [OD]) and lowest in HE rats
(0.58 /C6 0.17 OD), with intermediate values in HF rats
(0.78 /C6 0.15 OD, figure 5c). To further examine whether
high-fat fed and exenatide suppressed visfatin protein
level by downregulating its mRNA level, we examined
visfatin mRNA expression in adipose and muscle tis-
sues. However, mRNA levels of visfatin of both adipose
and muscle tissues were unchanged (data not shown).
Discussion
HFDs promote weight gain, insulin resistance and a state
of low-grade inflammation [24]. The main findings of the
current study were that a 6-week treatment with exena-
tide completely prevented the weight gain, the increase
in plasma FFA levels and insulin resistance, the
decrease in glucose tolerance and the fall in blood adi-
ponectin levels in HFD-treated rats. The mechanisms by
which exenatide produced all these effects were not
specifically investigated but were likely related to the
prevention of weight gain in the HFD-treated animals.
Exenatide has been firmly established to produce
weight loss [25,26]. There is good evidence to show that

exenatide and other GLP-1 agonists decrease food intake
by direct interaction with GLP-1 receptors in hypotha-
lamic centres that regulate appetite (Reviewed in 2). In
addition, exenatide can modify food intake by delaying
gastric emptying, which leads to early satiety and occa-
sionally to nausea [2]. Weight loss and a decrease in
plasma FFA levels are well known to improve insulin
sensitivity (reviewed in 27 and 28). Weight loss also
increases circulatory levels of adiponectin, which can
improve insulin action [29]. Our finding that exenatide
prevented HFD-induced decreases in IRS tyrosine phos-
phorylation supports the notion that weight loss and
lowering of FFA contributed to the beneficial effect of
this drug on insulin sensitivity [24,28].
We also observed a decrease in the metabolic clearance
rate of insulin in exenatide-treated rats. Reduced insulin
clearance has been reported in mice treated with GLP-1
and has been postulated to contribute to the increase in
systemic insulin levels typically found during GLP-1
administration [30]. However, newer studies have failed

to find a direct effect of GLP-1 on insulin clearance and
have suggested that the hyperinsulinaemia produced by
GLP-1 treatment was responsible for the decrease in
insulin clearance [31]. Inasmuch as exenatide treatment
improved both glucose-stimulated insulin secretion and
insulin action, the observed improvement in intrave-
nous glucose tolerance, therefore, was not surprising.
Thus, we believe that by preventing HFD-induced
weight gain, exenatide prevented the decrease in insulin
sensitivity and circulating levels of adiponectin and that
prevention of weight gain was the primary cause for the
observed beneficial effects on glucose homeostasis.
We also evaluated the effects of exenatide treatment on
adipocytokines by measuring the expression of visfatin
and adiponectin mRNA and their plasma protein levels.
Similar to our previous report in humans [32], the plasma
protein level of visfatin was significantly decreased in
the high fat–fed rats compared with NC rats. Interest-
ingly, after chronic administration of exenatide for
6 weeks, the plasma protein level of visfatin was fur-
ther decreased. Visfatin was found to exert insulin-
mimicking effects, bind to and activate the InsR without
competing with insulin [31]. Thus, it may be reasonable
to consider that visfatin protein is excessive expendi-
ture during developing insulin resistance and restoring
insulin sensitivity. Another potential explanation for
reducing circulating visfatin by chronic exenatide treat-
ment may be that visfatin protein synthesis was
restrained by increasing exenatide in vivo. Surprisingly,
visfatin mRNA expression in adipose and muscle
tissues remained unchanged among three groups. We
speculated that the effects of insulin resistance and exe-
natide on visfatin may occur at the post-transcriptional
level. However, further studies are necessary to eluci-
date the mechanisms underlying the changes of visfatin.
In summary, exenatide treatment for 6 weeks pre-
vented HFD-induced increases in body weight and dete-
rioration of insulin sensitivity, insulin secretion, glucose
tolerance and circulating plasma levels of FFA, triglycer-
ides and total cholesterol in high fat–fed rats. In addition,
exenatide increased adiponectin expression in adipose
tissue and skeletal muscle and raised circulating adipo-
nectin levels, which may have contributed to the
observed beneficial effects of exendin on insulin sensitiv-
ity and secretion.

第2页：双栏引言和研究方法页，介绍艾塞那肽的GLP-1受体作用、动物分组和给药方案；图1为正常饮食、高脂饮食及不同剂量艾塞那肽组的实验流程图。
第3页：双栏方法页，详述高胰岛素正常血糖钳夹、葡萄糖和胰岛素耐量试验、肝糖输出、基因表达、脂肪细胞因子及IRS-1磷酸化检测。
第4页：双栏方法末段和结果开端，说明Western blot、体成分和统计分析；表1比较各组体重、脂肪量、血糖、胰岛素、游离脂肪酸和血脂等基础指标。
第5页：图2由六个折线图组成，展示不同组静脉葡萄糖耐量试验中的血糖和胰岛素时间曲线，显示艾塞那肽改善高脂饮食造成的糖耐量异常。
第6页：图3包含四个胰岛素耐量试验血糖曲线；表2列正常血糖高胰岛素钳夹前后的血糖、胰岛素和游离脂肪酸，正文报告外周和肝脏胰岛素敏感性。
第7页：图4以柱状图和插图比较钳夹期间葡萄糖输注率、外周葡萄糖利用和肝糖生成；正文报告IRS-1、PI3K、GLUT4及脂肪细胞因子结果并开始讨论。
第8页：双栏讨论页，图5包含脂肪和肌肉IRS-1磷酸化的Western blot及定量图、血浆内脂素和脂联素表达图，展示艾塞那肽恢复胰岛素信号并提高脂联素。
第9页：双栏讨论与结论页，总结艾塞那肽通过体重、脂质、胰岛素信号和脂肪细胞因子改善高脂饮食诱导的胰岛素抵抗，随后为致谢和参考文献开端。
第10页：双栏参考文献末页，继续列出GLP-1、艾塞那肽、胰岛素敏感性及脂肪细胞因子相关研究。
